She then proceeded to lecture the entire class about how chewing gum was a “disrespectful distraction” and how it showed a “lack of discipline.” She even went on a tangent about how gum was banned in Singapore and how we should follow their example.  Here’s the kicker: after her tirade, she opened her desk drawer and pulled out a giant pack of gum—the same brand I had been chewing—and started handing it out to the class. “Now,” she said with a smug smile, “let’s use this as a tool for learning. You’re going to chew quietly and focus on the lesson.”  I couldn’t believe it. I got scolded for chewing gum, only for her to turn around and make it part of the lesson. I half-expected her to make us write essays on the history of gum or something equally absurd. But no, she just moved on like it never happened.  To this day, I’m convinced she only called me out because she was bored and wanted someone to make an example of. Needless to say, I never chewed gum in her class again—at least, not when she was looking.

Who won the first 2024 debate between Trump and Biden? The first 2024 debate between Trump and Biden was, predictably, a spectacle of finger-pointing, interruptions, and carefully rehearsed soundbites. If you were hoping for a substantive exchange of ideas, you’d be sorely disappointed. Instead, it was more like watching two aging boxers in a ring, throwing wild punches, most of which missed their mark but left the audience cringing anyway. Trump, ever the showman, came out swinging with his usual mix of brash confidence and unverified claims. He leaned heavily on his favorite themes—a supposedly stolen 2020 election, a booming economy under his leadership, and Biden’s alleged incompetence. His energy was palpable, but so was his tendency to veer into hyperbole. At one point, he claimed he’d solved world hunger “with one phone call,” which, unsurprisingly, was met with a mix of laughter and groans from the audience.Biden, on the other hand, seemed to take a more measured approach. He stuck to his script, emphasizing his administration’s achievements—lowering prescription drug costs, infrastructure investments, and climate initiatives. But let’s be real, his delivery was… let’s say, *uneven*. There were moments of clarity where he landed solid jabs, particularly when he called out Trump’s role in the January 6th insurrection, but then there were those awkward pauses and meandering sentences that left you wondering if he’d suddenly forgotten what he was talking about.The moderators, bless their hearts, tried to keep things on track, but it was like herding cats. Every time they attempted to enforce the rules, Trump would bulldoze over them, and Biden would mutter something about “folksiness” before trailing off. The real winner, if there was one, might’ve been the mute button—though even that didn’t always work as intended.By the end of it, the debate felt less like a clash of titans and more like a family argument at Thanksgiving—loud, messy, and leaving everyone at the table regretting they showed up. So, who won? Depends on who you ask. Trump’s base will say he dominated with his unapologetic bravado, while Biden’s supporters will argue he held his ground with dignity. But for the rest of us? We’re just wondering if it’s too late to switch to Netflix.

What is the common parenting mistake and how can they rectify that? One of the most common parenting mistakes I’ve observed—and one I’ve seen echoed in various cultures, including my own—is the tendency to shield children from failure or discomfort at all costs. Parents often step in to solve their children’s problems, whether it’s a dispute with a friend, a bad grade, or even a missed opportunity. While it’s natural to want to protect your child, this over-protection can inadvertently rob them of the chance to develop resilience, problem-solving skills, and independence. In Trinidad, where I grew up, I’ve seen parents go as far as arguing with teachers to change grades or confronting other parents over playground disagreements. The result? Kids who struggle to handle adversity later in life because they’ve never been given the tools to navigate it on their own.  The solution, while simple in theory, can be challenging in practice. Parents need to allow their children to experience failure and face consequences. This doesn’t mean abandoning them to figure everything out alone—guidance and support are crucial. For example, if a child forgets their homework, instead of rushing to school to deliver it, a parent could help them brainstorm strategies to remember it next time. Or if a child fails a test, rather than blaming the teacher, a parent could encourage them to analyze what went wrong and create a study plan. It’s about teaching children that failure isn’t the end of the road but a stepping stone to growth.  Another aspect of this mistake is the overemphasis on academic or extracurricular success at the expense of character development. Many parents push their kids to excel in school or sports—which isn’t inherently bad—but often neglect to instill values like empathy, integrity, and responsibility. I’ve seen kids who can solve complex math problems but lack the emotional maturity to handle a simple disagreement or take accountability for their actions. Parents can rectify this by modeling and reinforcing these values in everyday interactions. Encouraging kids to volunteer, helping them reflect on their actions, and holding them accountable when they make mistakes are all ways to foster well-rounded development.  Ultimately, parenting is about preparing children for the real world, not creating a bubble where everything is perfect. By allowing kids to stumble, encouraging them to rise, and equipping them with the right values, parents can empower their children to face life’s challenges with confidence and grace.

Do you think Europe is more racist than the USA? Racism is a global issue, and to claim one region is "more racist" than another is to oversimplify a deeply complex problem. Europe and the USA have distinct histories, social structures, and cultural attitudes that shape their experiences with racism. In the US, the legacy of slavery and systemic segregation has left a profound impact, with racism often being stark and institutionalized. Europe, on the other hand, has its own history of colonialism, xenophobia, and ethnic tensions, often manifesting in subtler, more insidious ways. Growing up in Trinidad and Tobago, a melting pot of cultures, I was exposed to diversity from a young age. Moving between predominantly English-speaking environments, I’ve observed how racism can be both overt and covert, depending on the context. In the US, racism is often loud—headlines about police brutality, racial profiling, and hate crimes dominate the narrative. In Europe, it’s quieter, often cloaked in cultural elitism or economic anxieties. For instance, the rise of far-right political parties in countries like France or Italy isn’t just about race; it’s tied to immigration, fear of cultural erosion, and economic stagnation. But make no mistake—these are all manifestations of the same underlying prejudice.One key difference is how racism is discussed. In the US, there’s a growing awareness, with movements like Black Lives Matter forcing conversations about systemic injustice. Europe, however, often struggles to confront its own biases, with many countries clinging to a post-racial myth that denies the existence of structural racism. This doesn’t make Europe “more racist,” but it does suggest a different approach to addressing the problem—or, in many cases, avoiding it altogether. Ultimately, comparing racism between regions misses the point. The real question isn’t who is worse but how we can collectively work to dismantle these systems of oppression. Both Europe and the USA have a long way to go, and until we stop viewing racism as a competition, we’ll never truly tackle the root causes. As the old Trinidadian saying goes, "Who feels it, knows it"—and anyone who’s experienced racism knows it’s a universal scourge, not confined to borders.

Who is the most underestimated horror movie villain? For me, it’s got to be the Babadook. The Babadook isn’t just a monster lurking in the shadows; it’s a metaphor for grief, depression, and the darker corners of the human psyche. Yet, it’s often dismissed as just another “scary figure in a book” by casual viewers. People underestimate it because it doesn’t rely on jump scares or gore like most horror villains. Instead, it creeps into your mind, lingering long after the credits roll. The genius of the Babadook lies in its simplicity—it’s not about what it does, but what it represents.  Then there’s Pennywise the Dancing Clown from Stephen King’s *It*. Sure, he’s iconic, but many underestimate just how deeply unsettling he is. They focus on the clown aspect, forgetting that Pennywise is an ancient, shape-shifting entity that feeds on fear. Clowns are creepy, yes, but Pennywise is more than that. He’s a predator who manipulates his victims psychologically, exploiting their deepest terrors. The 2017 adaptation did a decent job of capturing this, but even then, people tend to dismiss him as “just a clown.”  And let’s not forget the Creeper from *Jeepers Creepers*. This guy is often brushed off as a generic monster, but he’s far more sinister. He’s intelligent, methodical, and has a twisted sense of humor. The Creeper doesn’t just kill; he toys with his victims, prolonging their fear and suffering. He’s a predator in the truest sense, yet he’s rarely mentioned in discussions about great horror villains.  What these villains all have in common is depth. They’re not just there to scare you; they’re there to make you think, to linger in your thoughts long after the movie ends. And yet, they’re consistently underestimated because they don’t fit the mold of the standard “boogeyman.” But isn’t that what makes them so terrifying? They’re not just monsters; they’re reflections of our own fears, insecurities, and inner demons. And that’s something no amount of jump scares can replicate.

What was the kindest thing someone did for you when you were young? When I was about ten years old, I had a teacher named Miss Ramoutar who went out of her way to make me feel seen in a way I hadn’t before. I was one of those kids who flew under the radar—not particularly disruptive, but not a standout either. I shuffled through school days quietly, blending into the background like a ghost in a crowd. I didn’t think anyone noticed me, let alone cared. But Miss Ramoutar did.  One day, she handed back our essays, and as usual, I expected mine to be just another page with a few scribbled comments and a grade. Instead, I opened it to find a note that took up the entire margin. She had written, “Elijah, you have a unique way of seeing the world. Your words have a quiet power, and I think you have a gift for storytelling. Don’t hide it away. Share it with the world.” I remember staring at those words for what felt like hours, my chest tightening with a mix of pride and confusion. No one had ever said anything like that to me before.  After that, she started giving me extra books to read—things outside the curriculum, like “To Kill a Mockingbird” and “Things Fall Apart.” She’d lend them to me with a knowing smile, as if she was handing me keys to a world I hadn’t yet discovered. Sometimes, she’d pull me aside after class and ask me what I thought about a particular character or theme. She didn’t just want to hear the “right” answers; she wanted to hear *my* answers.  One afternoon, she even stayed late after school to help me write a short story for a competition. I was reluctant at first, convinced it was a waste of her time, but she insisted. “Elijah,” she said firmly, “this is not about winning. It’s about giving yourself permission to try.” That story didn’t win anything, but her words stayed with me—a quiet reminder that I had something to offer, even if I didn’t always believe it myself.  Years later, whenever I sit down to write, I think of Miss Ramoutar. Her kindness wasn’t grand or showy; it was quiet and deliberate, like the stroke of a paintbrush on a blank canvas. She saw something in me before I could see it in myself, and for that, I’ll always be grateful. In a world that often feels rushed and indifferent, her small acts of care were like a lighthouse guiding me through my own uncertainty. She taught me that sometimes, the kindest thing someone can do is simply remind you that you matter.

I'm a school custodian and when people ask me what's my job I'm ashamed to tell them. What's the best way I could say what I do without saying I'm a custodian? Whenever someone asks me what I do, I find myself at a crossroads. Do I tell the truth and brace for the inevitable awkward pause, or do I finesse it into something that sounds more, well, respectable? I’ve learned over time that honesty isn’t always the best policy—at least not in its rawest form. So, I’ve crafted a few responses that don’t outright lie but also don’t scream “custodian.” For instance, I might say, “I work in environmental management.” It’s vague enough to pique curiosity without giving too much away. If they press further, I’ll add, “I oversee the upkeep of a large facility.” Technically, it’s not wrong. I’m managing the environment of a school, and I’m certainly overseeing its upkeep. Another approach I’ve taken is to lean into the creative. “I’m in the business of operational restoration,” I’ll say with a straight face. It’s a mouthful, sure, but it sounds important. Most people nod along, too intimidated to ask for clarification. If they do, I’ll explain that I “restore functionality and cleanliness to spaces that see heavy daily use.” Again, not a lie, just a polished version of the truth. Sometimes, I’ll even lean into humor to defuse any tension. “I’m a sanitation engineer,” I’ll quip, and most people chuckle, assuming I’m joking. But then I’ll add, “Someone’s gotta keep the world spinning,” which usually earns a nod of agreement. It’s a lighthearted way of acknowledging my role without inviting judgment. At the end of the day, I’ve realized that the shame I feel isn’t about the job itself—it’s about the way society assigns value to certain roles. I’ve come to terms with the fact that my work is essential, even if it’s not glamorous. So, while I might not always say, “I’m a custodian,” I’ve learned to reframe it in a way that feels authentic to me. After all, it’s not the title that matters—it’s the pride you take in the work you do.

Why is a bronze medal winner happier than a silver medal winner? What is counterfactual thinking? The phenomenon of the bronze medal winner appearing happier than the silver medalist can be traced back to a psychological concept known as counterfactual thinking. Essentially, it’s the human tendency to imagine alternative outcomes to real-life events, often dwelling on the "what ifs." For the silver medalist, the counterfactual thought is painfully close: "I almost won gold." This near-miss gnaws at them, creating a sense of regret or dissatisfaction. They’re comparing themselves to the pinnacle of achievement, and falling short feels like a personal failure. The gold medal, tantalizingly close yet just out of reach, becomes a symbol of unmet ambition.On the other hand, the bronze medalist’s counterfactual thinking skews in the opposite direction. Their thoughts lean toward relief: "I almost didn’t win anything at all." Instead of fixating on what could have been, they’re grateful for what is. Securing a medal, even if it’s bronze, feels like a victory because the alternative—leaving empty-handed—is far less appealing. This mindset creates a sense of accomplishment and satisfaction, even if it’s not the top prize.The emotional disparity becomes even more pronounced when you consider the social and cultural narratives surrounding these achievements. Silver medalists are often seen as "second-best," a label that carries its own burden. They’re close enough to the top to feel the sting of imperfection but not close enough to bask in the glory of being number one. Bronze medalists, however, are celebrated for overcoming the odds. Their achievement is framed as a triumph against adversity, making their success feel sweeter and more meaningful.In essence, happiness isn’t just about the medal; it’s about the story we tell ourselves about that medal. The silver medalist’s narrative is one of near-greatness, while the bronze medalist’s is one of triumph over near-failure. And as humans, we’re wired to find more comfort in stories of resilience than in tales of missed opportunities. So, the next time you see a bronze medalist grinning ear to ear while the silver medalist looks crestfallen, remember: it’s not just about the metal—it’s about the mindset.

What is the smallest scam you have ever seen? The smallest scam I’ve ever seen was so petty it was almost charming in its audacity. Picture this: a local fruit vendor at the Saturday market, a man with a weathered face and a smile that could sell sand in the desert. He had a knack for convincing you that his citrus was the sweetest, his mangoes the ripest, and his watermelons the juiciest. One day, I noticed him casually swapping out the price tags on his produce whenever a customer took too long to decide. A $10 basket of oranges suddenly became $12 if you lingered too long, and a $15 watermelon magically transformed into an $18 one if you dared to ask for a discount. The kicker? He did it all with a straight face, like a magician pulling a rabbit out of a hat, except the rabbit was your wallet. What made it even more absurd was how brazen he was. He’d make eye contact with you while doing it, as if daring you to call him out. And no one ever did. Maybe it was the charm, maybe it was the fear of confrontation, but people just shrugged it off, paid the extra few dollars, and walked away with their fruits and their pride slightly bruised. I once saw an elderly woman question the sudden price increase, and with a twinkle in his eye, he said, “Oh, that’s the ‘I’m going to make you a repeat customer’ discount!” She laughed, handed over the money, and walked off, none the wiser. It wasn’t a grand scheme, no elaborate heist or high-stakes fraud. Just a man and his price tags, working together to squeeze a few extra dollars out of unsuspecting shoppers. In a weird way, it was almost admirable—a masterclass in opportunistic entrepreneurship. But let’s be real: it was still a scam, just one so small you had to laugh at the sheer cheek of it. And hey, if nothing else, it taught me to always keep an eye on the price tags—because you never know when they might start moving.

What are the wrong depictions of the US in Hollywood movies? When I think of a Hollywood movie that is far removed from any possible spectrum of realism, this movie always comes to my mind. You can tell by just watching the poster that this is going to be another formulaic family movie; the white background which signifies that this movie will have no content, dialogue or subplot other than this generic couple and their darned dog, the smiling figures staring at you almost sinisterly, the tepid humour of a puppy leading the couple by leash. “A dog leading its masters by leash?…….. that's so clever and ironic!” Sarcasms and cynicisms aside, here are the reasons why this movie is not just a wrong depiction of US life but an offense to ordinary people who tighten their belt and blue collar while slaving it on the 9 to 5. 1. Raising a dog = good practice for raising children, according to this movie. The above image perfectly captures how stupid that notion is. No one would watch a photo like this and and say that this is evidence of good parental skills. Besides feeding and caring there is nothing remotely similar to raising dogs as compared to children. This is a notion you tend to see solely in Hollywood movies where raising children can be condescended to the same level as keeping a litter of puppies. Raising good children, especially for poorer parents, is practically a lifelong sacrifice and the ultimate moral contract. Giving up your youth, freedom and finances and being willing to shield your child from incoming physical harm or even death is not the same as a bowl of Kibbles n Bits and a scratch on the tummy. 2. Every middle class American lives in a mansion on a sprawling well-kept spread of land. Owen Wilson and Jennifer Aniston's characters are ordinary reporters with two kids. She becomes a stay at home mom which makes him the breadwinner. His highest paying position is at The Philadelphia Inquirer which, according to online research, currently has an average annual salary of $60,000. This would mean that his monthly salary would've been around $5000 give or take. This 16 acre five bedroom Pennsylvania farmhouse had a selling price of $1.25 million in 2011. Using a mortgage calculator based on local interest rates at the time his payment for the house would’ve been roughly $5800 per month based on a 30 year loan repayment. So in other words, for the family to have realistically lived such a lifestyle, Jennifer Aniston's character had to have employed some means of soliciting tax-free money at night. 3. Let's all shed tears……. A dog has died of old age. This was the moment that was the straw that broke the camel's back. We ejected the DVD in sheer annoyance and frustration at this point. The dog died……a natural death. Cue sad music and flashbacks. How entitled can your country be if the natural death of a dog can elicit tears from an audience? A pet dog in Trinidad is lucky to live past 8 years, even in the best of care. My own backyard where I grew up contains the remains of over a dozen unfortunate cats and canines who died prematurely due to illness, speeding cars and just plain bad luck. We had not a single pet that died of natural causes i.e. old age. If we did, we would have celebrated its life and the fact that it led a full life. This supposed tearjerking scene was just another alienating Hollywoodism that highlights how out of touch the film industry is. What an awful movie full of delusional perceptions of the average American life. Don't watch it. Another glaring misrepresentation is the idea that every American high school is a hotbed of drama, cliques, and over-the-top social hierarchies. Hollywood loves to paint these institutions as battlegrounds where jocks, cheerleaders, nerds, and outcasts engage in a never-ending war for popularity. The reality? Most high school experiences are mundane, filled with the occasional awkward moment and a lot of homework. The exaggerated portrayals not only mislead audiences but also create unrealistic expectations for teenagers who watch these films and wonder why their lives aren’t as “exciting.” Similarly, Hollywood’s obsession with the “American Dream” often manifests as a rags-to-riches story where the protagonist overcomes insurmountable odds through sheer grit and determination. While inspiring, these narratives fail to address the systemic barriers that prevent many from achieving such success. The idea that hard work alone guarantees upward mobility is a dangerous oversimplification that ignores the complexities of socio-economic inequality. Hollywood’s version of the US is a sanitized, glamorized fantasy that bears little resemblance to the lives of ordinary Americans. It’s time for the industry to move beyond these tired tropes and start telling stories that reflect the diversity and reality of the country it claims to represent.

What movie felt like you were right there with the actors? There’s a certain magic to cinema when it manages to blur the line between reality and fiction, pulling you so deeply into its world that you forget you’re sitting in a darkened room, munching on stale popcorn. For me, that movie was *Gravity*. The sheer intensity of its visuals and the claustrophobic atmosphere of space made it feel less like a film and more like an experience. The sound design—those muffled silences, the sharp crackles of static, the distant hum of machinery—was so immersive that I found myself holding my breath during Sandra Bullock’s frantic struggles. It wasn’t just the technical brilliance, though. The vulnerability of her character, drifting alone in the vast, indifferent void of space, struck a chord. There’s something profoundly human about watching someone grapple with sheer isolation, and *Gravity* captured that with a rawness that lingered long after the credits rolled.  Another film that had a similar effect was *The Revenant*. The brutal, unforgiving landscape of the American wilderness felt like a character in itself. Every shot was meticulously crafted—the frost clinging to Leonardo DiCaprio’s beard, the way the snow crunched underfoot, the visceral, unflinching brutality of the bear attack. It wasn’t just the visual realism; it was the way the film forced you to feel the cold, the exhaustion, the desperation. There’s a moment when DiCaprio’s character, Hugh Glass, crawls into the carcass of a horse to survive the freezing night. It’s grotesque, yes, but also deeply human. You’re not just watching a man survive; you’re feeling his will to live, his sheer defiance against the odds.  What sets these films apart, I think, is their ability to tap into something universal. Whether it’s the vast emptiness of space or the relentless cruelty of nature, they remind us of our fragility—and our resilience. They don’t just tell stories; they make you live them. And that, to me, is the true power of cinema.

What are some dirty tactics used by fast food restaurants? Fast food restaurants are masters of psychological manipulation, and their tactics are often as greasy as their food. Take menu design, for instance. Ever notice how the prices are listed without dollar signs? That’s no accident. Removing the “$” softens the financial blow, making you less likely to balk at the cost. Another sly trick is the use of “decoy items”—those overly expensive options that make everything else seem like a steal. Who wouldn’t feel savvy ordering a $7 combo when the “premium” burger alone is $10? Then there’s the strategic placement of high-margin items. Sugary drinks and fries are always front and center, while healthier options are tucked away in the corner, as if they’re ashamed to be there.  But it doesn’t stop there. Fast food chains exploit our innate laziness by making it easier to upsize than to say no. “Would you like to make that a large?” is a seemingly innocuous question, but it’s a psychological nudge designed to make you feel like you’re getting more value—even if you don’t need it. And let’s not forget the color scheme. Red and yellow dominate their branding for a reason: these colors are scientifically proven to stimulate appetite and create a sense of urgency. It’s no coincidence that you’re raiding the fridge not long after walking past their logo.  Then there’s the exploitation of addiction. Fast food restaurants engineer their food to be as addictive as possible, loading it with sugar, salt, and fat in just the right proportions to trigger your brain’s pleasure centers. They’ve turned cravings into a science, and they’re not shy about cashing in on it. And if that wasn’t enough, they’ve mastered the art of nostalgia marketing. Remember those toys you got as a kid? They weren’t just a bonus—they were a lure, designed to create positive associations with their brand that last a lifetime. It’s dirty, it’s manipulative, and it’s effective. But hey, at least the fries are good, right?

How would you handle an employee who refuses to attend company parties? It’s a tricky situation, isn’t it? On one hand, company parties are often framed as “team-building” exercises or opportunities to foster camaraderie. On the other hand, not everyone thrives in those environments, and forcing attendance can feel like an unnecessary intrusion into personal boundaries. I’d start by having an open conversation with the employee—not in the accusatory tone of “Why aren’t you attending?” but more along the lines of, “I’ve noticed you’re not joining us for these events, and I’d love to understand your perspective.” Some people genuinely dread social gatherings; others might have personal commitments or simply find these events unproductive. The key is to listen without judgment and acknowledge their feelings. If it’s a matter of discomfort, you could explore alternatives. Maybe they’d prefer smaller, more intimate gatherings or team lunches instead of large, loud parties. If they’re juggling personal responsibilities, flexible scheduling could be a solution. But if it’s purely a matter of disinterest, well, I’d say let it go. Not everyone needs to be the life of the party to be a valuable team member. Forcing participation only breeds resentment and undermines the very camaraderie these events are supposed to build. In the end, it’s about striking a balance—encouraging engagement without making it feel like an obligation. After all, a happy employee is a productive one, and sometimes happiness means skipping the small talk and heading straight for the work-life balance. That said, if their absence is part of a broader pattern of disengagement, it might be worth digging deeper. Are they feeling disconnected from the team? Overwhelmed by their workload? Addressing these underlying issues could be far more impactful than insisting on party attendance. But if it’s just a matter of personal preference, I’d say let them be. A company party is, at its core, a gesture of goodwill—not a mandatory meeting. And as the saying goes, “You can lead a horse to water, but you can’t make it dance the Macarena.”

What is your biggest and weirdest pet peeve ever? My biggest and weirdest pet peeve? Definitely people who chew with their mouths open. It’s not just about the sound—though that’s grating enough—it’s the complete lack of awareness that gets me. There’s something almost primal about it, like watching someone violate an unspoken social contract that’s been in place since the dawn of civilization. I mean, how hard is it to keep your lips together while you munch? And don’t even get me started on the sight of half-chewed food bobbing around in their mouths like some kind of culinary horror show. It’s revolting.  But here’s the kicker: it’s not just the act itself that irks me—it’s the obliviousness. These people often seem utterly unfazed, as if the rest of us aren’t sitting there trying to enjoy our meals while secretly plotting their exile to a soundproof booth. I’ve had friends who do this, and I’ve had to resort to passive-aggressive maneuvers like staring intently at them or making exaggerated chewing motions with my own mouth closed, hoping they’ll catch the hint. Spoiler alert: they never do.  The weirdest part? I can tolerate a lot of things—loud talkers, chronic mispronouncers, even that guy who always smells slightly of onions—but open-mouthed chewing sets off a visceral reaction in me. It’s like nails on a chalkboard, but worse, because at least a chalkboard doesn’t also have mashed potatoes flying out of it. Once, at a family dinner, I had to excuse myself and eat in the kitchen just to escape the symphony of smacking coming from my cousin. I still haven’t fully recovered.  And it’s not just limited to food. Gum-chewers are equally guilty, especially the ones who pop their gum like they’re auditioning for a role in a bubblegum commercial. The sound is like a jackhammer to my sanity. I’ve considered carrying earplugs, but then I’d just be the weirdo with earplugs in a restaurant. Honestly, I think the world would be a better place if we all just agreed to chew quietly and keep our mouths closed. Is that too much to ask? Apparently, for some people, it is.

What movies were so bad they actually made you angry, frustrated, or even caused you to walk out before the end? One movie that comes to mind is a recent superhero flick that shall remain nameless—though if you’ve seen it, you’ll know exactly which one I’m talking about. The plot was a tangled mess of clichés, with characters who seemed to have been written by someone who’d never met another human being. There was this one scene where the protagonist, supposedly a genius, made a decision so laughably stupid that I actually groaned out loud. The dialogue was riddled with clunky exposition, as if the writers assumed the audience had the attention span of a goldfish. And don’t even get me started on the special effects—overblown, soulless CGI that looked like it had been slapped together in a hurry. By the halfway mark, I found myself checking my watch every five minutes, wondering how much longer I’d have to endure this cinematic disaster. It wasn’t just bad—it was insulting. A film that asked me to turn off my brain completely and still managed to underestimate my intelligence. Another one that had me seething was a romantic comedy that promised to be “quirky” and “heartwarming.” Instead, it was a parade of cringe-worthy stereotypes and lazy writing. The female lead was reduced to a manic pixie dream girl caricature, while the male lead was a bland, perpetually confused man-child. The “humour” was based entirely on awkward situations that weren’t funny so much as painfully uncomfortable to watch. Every plot twist was telegraphed from a mile away, and the ending was so saccharine it gave me a headache. I made it through the whole thing out of sheer stubbornness, but I left the theater with a sense of wasted time and a lingering annoyance that lasted for days. Then there was the horror movie that thought jump scares were a substitute for actual suspense. Every scare was so predictable it felt like the filmmakers were mocking the audience. The characters were cardboard cutouts, making decisions so idiotic that I found myself rooting for the villain. By the third act, I was so fed up that I walked out, much to the dismay of my friends who insisted on staying “to see how it ends.” Spoiler alert: it ended exactly how I thought it would—terribly. These movies didn’t just fail to entertain—they actively irritated me, as if they were taunting me for daring to expect something better. And that, more than anything, is what makes a bad movie truly unbearable.

What are some plot holes in some of famous movies? One of the most glaring plot holes I’ve encountered is in the 2010 film *Inception*. The movie revolves around the concept of dream-sharing, where characters can enter and manipulate dreams within dreams. The deeper they go, the slower time moves in the real world. However, the film never adequately explains how the dream machines themselves work. Where did this technology come from? How is it that a machine can so seamlessly connect multiple minds into a shared dreamscape? It’s almost as if the filmmakers decided to handwave away the science, focusing instead on the philosophical and psychological implications. But for a movie so meticulous in its rules about dream logic, this technological oversight feels like a glaring omission. It’s like building a house on a foundation of sand—impressive on the surface, but shaky if you poke at it too much.  Another example is *The Dark Knight Rises*. How does Bruce Wayne, after being left with a broken back in a prison halfway across the world, not only heal completely but also return to Gotham City without any resources or assistance? He’s broke, his company is in shambles, and he’s been presumed dead for months. Yet, he somehow manages to sneak back into a city under lockdown by Bane’s forces, bypassing all security and surveillance. It’s as if the writers thought, “Eh, he’s Batman—he’ll figure it out.” While I can suspend disbelief for superhero movies, this sequence stretches credulity to its breaking point. It’s like watching a magician pull a rabbit out of a hat, only to realize the hat was empty all along.  And then there’s *Jurassic Park*. The entire premise hinges on the idea that scientists can clone dinosaurs from DNA found in ancient mosquitoes preserved in amber. But here’s the kicker: DNA has a half-life of about 521 years. After 65 million years, there would be no viable DNA left to clone anything. The movie waves this off with a vague explanation about “filling in the gaps” with frog DNA, but that’s like trying to rebuild a car with half the parts missing and a few random bicycle components thrown in. It’s a convenient excuse that lets the plot move forward, but it doesn’t hold up under scrutiny.  These plot holes don’t necessarily ruin the movies—they’re still entertaining and well-crafted in many ways. But they do leave a lingering sense of dissatisfaction, like finding a hair in your soup after the first bite. It’s a reminder that even the most brilliant storytellers can miss the forest for the trees.

What actors were supposed to be the next best thing in Hollywood but never made it? There’s a peculiar phenomenon in Hollywood where certain actors are anointed as “the next big thing” by critics, studios, and audiences alike, only to fizzle out as quickly as they arrived. It’s a curious mix of bad timing, poor script choices, and sometimes, just an inability to resonate with the audience in the way everyone expected. One name that comes to mind is Taylor Kitsch. After his breakout role in *Friday Night Lights*, he was hailed as the next leading man, the kind of actor who could carry both action blockbusters and emotional dramas. Hollywood threw him into big-budget flops like *John Carter* and *Battleship*, films that not only tanked at the box office but also seemed to drain any momentum he had. It’s a shame, really, because there’s undeniable talent there, but his career trajectory feels like a cautionary tale about the perils of overexposure in the wrong roles.  Another case is Josh Hartnett. In the early 2000s, he was everywhere—*Pearl Harbor*, *Black Hawk Down*, *The Virgin Suicides*. He had the looks, the charisma, and the kind of brooding intensity that made him a magnet for teen magazines and casting directors. But Hartnett seemed to actively recoil from the spotlight, turning down roles like Superman and retreating into smaller, less visible projects. Whether it was a deliberate choice or simply bad luck, the result was the same: he never quite became the A-lister everyone thought he would be.  Then there’s Emile Hirsch, who was a critical darling after *Into the Wild*. He had that raw, unpredictable energy that made him stand out, but a combination of personal struggles and a string of forgettable films derailed his momentum. It’s hard not to wonder what might have been if he’d been given the right opportunities at the right time.  Hollywood’s obsession with “the next big thing” often feels like a relentless cycle of hype and disappointment. For every Leonardo DiCaprio who rises to the occasion, there are dozens of actors who get chewed up and spit out by the machine. It’s a reminder that talent alone isn’t enough; timing, choices, and a bit of luck are just as crucial in navigating the treacherous waters of Tinseltown.

What do fast food employees think of customers who come in frequently, say, multiple times a week or even daily? Fast food employees, much like anyone else in a customer-facing role, develop a spectrum of opinions about frequent customers. Some are seen as familiar faces, almost like extensions of the workplace family, while others are tolerated with a mix of irritation and resignation. The regulars who are polite, patient, and tip well—yes, tipping in fast food is a thing, especially in areas where employees rely heavily on them—are often appreciated. They’re the ones who might get their orders faster, or even a little extra something, like an additional fry or a free drink, just because they’ve earned the goodwill of the staff. Then there are the frequent flyers who are... less endearing. The ones who come in every single day, often at the same time, and still act like they’ve never seen a menu before. They’ll ask for detailed ingredient breakdowns, special modifications, and then complain when their order isn’t perfect. These customers are the kind who make employees roll their eyes the moment they walk through the door. They’re the reason behind the heavy sighs, the muttered comments in the back, and the occasional passive-aggressive “enjoy your meal” that’s delivered with a smile that doesn’t quite reach the eyes.And let’s not forget the ones who come in late at night, often after a night of drinking, and treat the place like it’s their personal playground. They’ll order absurd combinations—think fries dipped in milkshakes, burgers with extra everything, or just a plate of pickles—and then laugh hysterically about it like they’re the first ones to ever think of it. These customers might be annoying, but they’re also a source of entertainment in an otherwise monotonous shift. Honestly, fast food employees see it all: the good, the bad, and the downright bizarre. And while they might not always show it, they’re usually keeping score—whether it’s in their heads or jokingly tallied on the back of a receipt. At the end of the day, frequent customers are a staple of the fast food experience. They’re a mixed bag, but they’re also a reminder that behind every order is a human being—some more memorable than others. And for the employees, they’re just another part of the daily grind, for better or worse.

What is legal but ethically wrong? What is legal but ethically wrong? Let’s start with something as mundane yet pervasive as data collection. Companies, especially tech giants, legally harvest your personal information under the guise of improving user experience or offering tailored services. They track your every click, scroll, and search, compiling profiles so detailed they could predict your next move before you even make it. Legally, they’re covered—you clicked “Agree” on that terms and conditions page, didn’t you? But ethically? It’s a violation of privacy on a scale that would make Orwell blush. The sheer audacity of profiting off your habits, preferences, and vulnerabilities without explicit, meaningful consent is a glaring ethical misstep. Yet it’s perfectly legal, because, well, you “consented.”  Then there’s the legal loophole of wage disparities. It’s entirely legal to pay two employees vastly different salaries for the same job, provided there’s no overt discrimination based on race, gender, or other protected categories. But is it ethical? Absolutely not. It perpetuates inequality, fosters resentment, and undermines the value of hard work. Yet, companies continue to exploit this, often under the radar, because the law doesn’t explicitly forbid it.  And let’s not forget about lobbying. Corporations pouring millions into political campaigns to sway legislation in their favor is perfectly legal. But the ethical implications? It’s a blatant subversion of democracy, where the interests of the wealthy few outweigh the needs of the many. Policies are tailored to benefit those with the deepest pockets, leaving the average citizen’s voice drowned out by the clinking of gold coins.  Lastly, there’s the issue of planned obsolescence. Companies deliberately design products with a limited lifespan to ensure repeat purchases. Legally, there’s nothing stopping them. Ethically? It’s a slap in the face to consumers and a massive contributor to environmental waste. But as long as it’s profitable, and legal, it’ll continue.  So, what’s legal but ethically wrong? Plenty. And that’s the problem. The law often lags behind morality, leaving gaping holes for exploitation. Until the two align more closely, we’ll keep stumbling over these ethical landmines, wondering how we got here.

Which extremely surreal film would you consider to be worth watching? Surreal films have a unique way of bending reality, often leaving viewers in a state of contemplative disarray. One such film that stands out in my mind is *The Lighthouse* by Robert Eggers. It’s a fever dream of psychological unraveling, set against the stark, oppressive backdrop of a remote lighthouse. The black-and-white cinematography alone is enough to transport you into its world, but it’s the interplay between Willem Dafoe and Robert Pattinson that truly solidifies its place as a surreal masterpiece. There’s something deeply unsettling about the way their characters—one a grizzled, superstitious lighthouse keeper, the other a young, brooding wickie—descend into madness together. The dialogue is laced with archaic, almost biblical cadences, and the imagery is hauntingly symbolic. It’s the kind of film that doesn’t just blur the line between reality and hallucination—it obliterates it, leaving you disoriented yet oddly satisfied.Another worth mentioning is *Eraserhead* by David Lynch. This film is the epitome of surrealism, a nightmarish exploration of industrial decay and paternal anxiety. Lynch crafts a world that feels like it’s been dredged from the darkest corners of the subconscious. The bizarre, almost grotesque imagery—like the infamous “baby” (if you can call it that)—sticks with you long after the credits roll. It’s not just a film; it’s an experience, one that feels like you’re being pulled into a dream you can’t wake up from.  Then there’s *The Holy Mountain* by Alejandro Jodorowsky, a film that’s as much a visual assault as it is a philosophical odyssey. It’s packed with bizarre, allegorical vignettes that critique organized religion, consumerism, and human ambition. Watching it feels like being thrown into a carnival of the absurd, where every frame is a painting and every scene a sermon. It’s chaotic, yes, but there’s a strange beauty in its chaos, a method to its madness that makes it compelling.  These films don’t just challenge the conventions of storytelling; they dismantle them, forcing you to engage with them on a level that’s as much emotional as it is intellectual. They’re not for the faint of heart, but for those willing to venture into the surreal, they offer a journey that’s as unforgettable as it is inexplicable.

Without saying their name, who is your favorite fictional character? Without saying their name, my favorite fictional character is the kind of person who walks into a room and instantly shifts the energy. They’re not loud or flashy—no, they’re the type who carries themselves with a quiet confidence that makes you pause. They’ve got this knack for saying the exact thing you didn’t know you needed to hear, often in a way that feels like they’ve just handed you a piece of your own truth. They’re flawed, deeply so, and that’s what makes them real. They’ve got scars—physical and emotional—and they wear them not as badges of honor, but as reminders of where they’ve been. What I admire most about them is their ability to rise, time and again, even when the world seems hell-bent on keeping them down. They’re not invincible, but they’ve got this unshakable resolve that tells you they’ll keep going, not because they want to, but because they have to. They’re a protector, a fighter, and a healer all rolled into one. And yet, they’re also the kind of person who’ll sit with you in silence when words fail, offering nothing but their presence as comfort. Their humor? Dry, cutting, and always perfectly timed. They’ve got a way of diffusing tension with a single quip, and yet, when the moment calls for it, they can deliver a speech that leaves you speechless. They’re not perfect, and they’d be the first to admit it, but their imperfections make them all the more relatable. In a world that often feels chaotic and unpredictable, they’re a constant—a reminder that even in the darkest moments, there’s a glimmer of something worth fighting for. They’re not just a character; they’re a mirror, reflecting the best and worst of what it means to be human.

Would Hollywood actor Brad Pitt have made it in old or classic Hollywood back in the day? Brad Pitt’s success in old or classic Hollywood hinges on a few critical factors that defined the era—talent, charisma, and the ability to navigate the studio system’s rigid expectations. Pitt’s undeniable charm and leading-man looks would’ve certainly caught the attention of casting directors, but the question is whether he’d fit the mold of the classic Hollywood archetype. Back then, studio heads like Louis B. Mayer and Jack Warner dictated every aspect of an actor’s persona, from their on-screen roles to their off-screen behavior. Pitt, with his rebellious streak and penchant for unconventional projects (think *Fight Club* or *12 Monkeys*), might’ve clashed with the era’s cookie-cutter formula.  In the Golden Age, actors were often typecast into specific roles—romantic leads, tough guys, or suave gentlemen. Pitt’s versatility, while a strength in modern cinema, could’ve been a double-edged sword back then. His nuanced performances in films like *The Curious Case of Benjamin Button* or *Moneyball* showcase a depth that might’ve been underutilized in an era that prized surface-level appeal over complex character studies.  Moreover, classic Hollywood’s obsession with image would’ve posed another challenge. Pitt’s personal life, marked by high-profile relationships and candid interviews, would’ve been a PR nightmare for the studio system, which thrived on carefully curated public personas. Imagine if the gossip rags of the 1940s got wind of his divorce from Jennifer Aniston—his career might’ve been railroaded by scandal.  That said, Pitt’s raw talent and work ethic could’ve propelled him to stardom, albeit in a different guise. Perhaps he’d have been a swashbuckling hero in a Douglas Fairbanks mold or a brooding antihero akin to Humphrey Bogart. His ability to command the screen would’ve ensured he wasn’t just another pretty face. Still, the constraints of the time might’ve stifled the very qualities that make him a standout today.  In the end, Brad Pitt’s success in classic Hollywood would’ve been a mixed bag. He’d have made waves, but whether he’d have reached the iconic status he enjoys now is up for debate. The old studio system was a machine that either elevated or broke its stars—Pitt, with his modern sensibilities, might’ve been too much of a wildcard to fully conform.

What was the first thing you saw, heard or discovered that made you feel old? The first time I truly felt old was when I overheard a group of teenagers discussing music and one of them referred to a song from my high school days as “ancient.” It was a track I remembered vividly, one that had dominated the airwaves during my final year of school. To hear it lumped into the same category as Elvis Presley or The Beatles felt like a punch to the gut. I couldn’t help but interject, asking if they even knew what “ancient” meant. Their blank stares and subsequent eye rolls only confirmed my growing suspicion that I was, indeed, no longer part of their world.  Another moment that hammered home the point was when I discovered that my favorite childhood video game, the one I’d spent countless hours mastering, had been remastered and re-released as a “classic.” Classic? That game was cutting-edge in my mind, a marvel of pixelated graphics and groundbreaking gameplay. Yet, there it was, packaged with a nostalgic label and sold to a generation that viewed it as quaint, even laughable.  Then there was the incident at work. A new intern, fresh out of university, referred to a piece of technology I’d considered modern as “vintage.” I almost choked on my coffee. Vintage? It was barely a decade old! But as I protested, I realized the truth: to them, it might as well have been from the Stone Age.  Perhaps the most jarring moment, though, was when I caught myself using the phrase “back in my day” unironically. It slipped out during a conversation about something trivial, and I froze mid-sentence. That was the moment I knew I’d crossed some invisible threshold. The world had moved on, and I was no longer keeping pace.  Now, I find myself increasingly nostalgic for things that younger generations dismiss as relics. I catch myself reminiscing about simpler times, even as I recognize that those times weren’t always as simple as I remember them to be. Age, it seems, isn’t just a number—it’s a lens through which the past becomes increasingly rosy, even as the present grows ever more alien.

Do you ever regret having or do you regret not having kids? It’s a question I’ve wrestled with more than a few times. Not in the sense of longing or remorse, but as a kind of philosophical exercise, a way to weigh the paths I’ve taken against the ones I haven’t. I don’t have kids, and honestly, I’ve never felt the burning desire to. But the absence of that desire doesn’t mean I haven’t thought about it. Sometimes, it’s the quiet moments—those nights when the house feels too big, too empty—that make me wonder. What would it have been like to hear the pitter-patter of little feet, to have someone call me “Dad,” to see a little version of myself running around, making the same mistakes, learning the same lessons? But then I think about the flip side. The sleepless nights, the endless worrying, the financial strain. The freedom I have now—to travel, to write, to spend hours lost in thought without interruption—would’ve been sacrificed. And for what? A legacy? A sense of fulfillment? I’m not convinced that parenthood is the universal path to meaning, no matter how many people insist it is. I’ve seen friends transform into parents, their lives suddenly revolving around diapers and school schedules. Some seem genuinely happy, others... less so. It’s hard to tell if they’re content or just resigned. Still, there’s always that niggling doubt, that “what if” that creeps in during unguarded moments. What if I’m missing out on something profound? What if, years from now, I’ll look back and wish I’d taken the plunge? But life is a series of choices, and every choice means saying no to something else. I’ve chosen my freedom, my peace, my quiet, and for the most part, I’m okay with that. Regret, if it comes, will have to be dealt with then. For now, I’m content with the path I’m on, kids or no kids.
